name: Setup quality
definition: A grade of how well a specific trade opportunity matches the trader's validated setups and current market conditions - in proprietary-trading practice expressed as tiers (A/B/C) that gate size and frequency. It operationalizes selectivity: capital concentrates on the highest-quality instances of proven patterns.
intuition: Not every valid-looking pattern deserves the same money; an A-setup in the right market is a different bet from a marginal lookalike.
mechanics: Playbook setups are scored before entry against confluence factors (trend, level, volume, catalyst, time of day, the setup's recent tracked performance); the grade determines whether to trade and how much to risk. Bellafiore's SMB framework ties grade to conviction and size, and grades are audited in daily review.
failure_modes: Grades drift under emotion: after losses everything looks like a C, after wins everything looks like an A. Grading without historical per-setup expectancy data is subjective relabeling, not measurement.
misconceptions: Quality is a property of the setup-context match, not of how confident or excited the trader feels. Skipping B and C setups is not cowardice - it is how expectancy is protected when edges are thin.
example: A pullback-to-VWAP long in a strong trend after earnings grades A and gets full size; the same pattern in a choppy midday tape grades C and is skipped.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: Rule adherence
definition: The degree to which actual trading behavior matches the written rules of the trading plan - entries, exits, sizing, and risk limits taken as specified, with deviations logged. It is the primary process metric of trading discipline.
intuition: The system only works if the operator runs it; rule adherence measures whether you ran your system or your mood.
mechanics: Each trade is scored rule by rule (valid setup, correct size, stop honored, exit per plan); the adherence rate is the share of fully compliant trades. Deviations are classified (early entry, moved stop, oversized, revenge trade) and tracked over time in the journal.
formula: Rule adherence (%) = (number of trades fully compliant with plan rules) / (total trades) x 100.
failure_modes: High adherence to a bad system yields consistent losses - adherence measures fidelity, not edge. Rules written with ambiguity cannot be scored, which makes adherence unmeasurable and review toothless.
misconceptions: Perfect adherence is not rigidity: planned, documented rule changes made in review are part of the process, while improvising mid-trade is not. A winning trade that broke rules counts as an adherence failure, not a success.
example: A trader's month shows 22 of 25 trades fully compliant (88%); the three violations - all moved stops - account for 60% of the month's drawdown.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: Execution error
definition: A mistake in implementing an intended trade - wrong order type or price, fat-fingered size, missed or late entry, early or late exit relative to plan - as distinct from a flawed idea. It is measured as the gap between intended and actual execution.
intuition: The analysis was right and the plan was right; the fingers or the timing were wrong.
mechanics: Detected by comparing each trade to its plan: slippage versus expected fill, entry timing versus trigger, exit versus exit rule. Sources include inattention, platform errors, latency, and emotional hesitation; mitigations are checklists, hotkeys with size limits, and rehearsed order routines.
failure_modes: Execution errors are most frequent exactly when markets are fastest and stakes highest; in leveraged instruments a single size or order-type error can exceed all planned risk. They are undercounted unless intent is recorded before the trade.
misconceptions: A profitable fat-finger is still an error, not a win; grading by outcome hides the defect. Small repeated execution leaks (late entries, chasing fills) compound into a large expectancy drag even when each instance seems trivial.
example: Intending a limit buy at 50.00 with a 49.50 stop, a trader market-buys at 50.35 in a spike; the extra 0.35 of slippage turns a planned 2:1 trade into 1.4:1 before it starts.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: Analysis error
definition: A flaw in the reasoning or information processing behind a trade - misread trend, wrong level, ignored evidence, miscalibrated probability - as distinct from an execution mistake or a risk-management breach. It is the error class that review and education, rather than checklists, must fix.
intuition: You did exactly what you planned; the problem is the plan was built on a misread chart.
mechanics: Identified in post-trade and decision-journal review by comparing the recorded thesis with the information available at the time: cognitive biases (confirmation, anchoring, recency), data errors, and logical gaps are the usual culprits. Persistent analysis errors point to gaps in market understanding or to a systematic bias.
failure_modes: Hindsight bias makes analysis errors hard to diagnose honestly - the misread is rewritten as nearly right. Small samples confound signal: a correct analysis can lose and a wrong one can win several times in a row.
misconceptions: A losing trade is not automatically an analysis error - sound analysis of a probabilistic setup still loses its share of times. Conversely, a winning trade built on misread information is still an analysis error, not validation.
example: A trader shorts into what he reads as distribution, ignoring that the decline is on falling volume into a major demand zone; review tags it as an analysis error: context filter omitted.

citations.source: Brett N. Steenbarger, The Psychology of Trading: Tools and Techniques for Minding the Markets (Wiley, 2003) - publisher page

name: Risk-management error
definition: A breach of the rules that bound loss - oversizing, moving or removing stops, exceeding daily loss limits, adding to losers, or ignoring correlation between positions. It is the most dangerous error class because it converts bounded, survivable mistakes into account-threatening losses.
intuition: You can be wrong a hundred times and survive if risk is controlled; one risk-management error at the wrong leverage can end the account.
mechanics: Measured by comparing realized per-trade and per-day losses and exposures against plan limits and against risk capacity; violations are tagged in the journal and reviewed separately from P&L. Defenses are structural: hard stops, platform-enforced size and loss limits, and sizing formulas tied to invalidation distance.
failure_modes: These errors cluster during tilt and after losses, when the urge to recover overrides limits; they are also hidden by luck - oversized bets that win teach the wrong lesson until variance collects. Correlated positions make nominal diversification illusory.
misconceptions: Risk management is not a drag on returns bolted onto the strategy; sizing and exits are part of the strategy's expectancy. A stop that was never hit by luck does not prove the oversize was safe.
example: Plan caps risk at 0.5% per trade and 1.5% per day; during a news spike the trader doubles size and lifts the stop, taking a 4% hit - logged in review as a risk-management error, the category the plan exists to prevent.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Table of contents, Ch. 6 'Live to Play Another Day'

citations.source: Wikipedia: Risk appetite (ISO 31000 vocabulary)

name: Process metric
definition: A quantitative measure of how well the trading process was executed - rule-adherence rate, setup-selection grade distribution, slippage versus plan, review completion - independent of whether individual trades won or lost. Process metrics make discipline measurable and correct for outcome bias in self-evaluation.
intuition: P&L tells you what the market did; process metrics tell you what you did.
mechanics: Derived from the journal and execution data: percentage of trades on valid playbook setups, stops honored, planned size used, entries within the trigger window, checklist completion. Tracked weekly and monthly to detect behavioral drift before it shows up in the equity curve.
failure_modes: Metrics get gamed (Goodhart's law): traders contort behavior to hit adherence percentages while hollowing out their meaning. Process metrics also cannot validate the strategy itself - perfect process on zero edge still loses.
misconceptions: Process metrics are not vanity statistics; they are leading indicators because process degradation precedes P&L degradation. They also do not replace outcome metrics - the two are read together.
example: A trader tracks: 94% of trades on playbook setups, 100% of stops honored, average entry slippage 0.04 - and treats a dip in any of them as a warning independent of the month's profit.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Table of contents, Ch. 9 'Maximizing Your Profits with Scoring'

name: Outcome metric
definition: A measure of trading results - net P&L, expectancy, win rate, average R-multiple, drawdown, risk-adjusted return - capturing what the strategy earned rather than how it was executed. Outcome metrics are the ultimate test of a process but are noisy and must not be read trade by trade.
intuition: Outcomes are the scoreboard, but over any small number of games the scoreboard mostly measures luck.
mechanics: Computed from closed trades: expectancy combines win rate with average win and loss sizes; R-distributions, maximum drawdown, and risk-adjusted returns complete the picture. Interpreted over adequate samples and paired with process metrics to attribute results to skill, system, or variance.
formula: Expectancy E = p_w * W_avg - p_l * L_avg, where p_w = win rate, W_avg = average win, p_l = loss rate, L_avg = average loss (in R-multiples or currency).
failure_modes: Short-horizon outcome metrics are dominated by variance: dozens to hundreds of trades may be needed before expectancy estimates stabilize. Maximizing outcome metrics directly invites overfitting, hidden tail risk, and outcome-biased self-assessment.
misconceptions: A profitable month does not prove a process improvement, and a losing month does not disprove one - sample size governs what outcome metrics can say. A high win rate alone is meaningless without the sizes of wins and losses.
example: Over 200 journaled trades a system shows a 42% win rate, average win 2.3R, average loss 1.0R - expectancy about +0.39R per trade, a positive edge invisible in any single week.

citations.source: Wikipedia: Outcome bias
Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: A-trade
definition: In the setup-grading taxonomy used in proprietary trading (popularized by Mike Bellafiore's SMB framework), the highest grade of opportunity: a trade matching the trader's best playbook patterns under favorable conditions, warranting full planned position size. The grade is a sizing decision based on the pattern class's tracked expectancy, not a claim about certainty.
intuition: An A-trade is the one you trained for - your best pattern, in the right market, at the right time; that is where size belongs.
mechanics: Setups are graded before entry against confluence criteria (pattern quality, trend, volume, catalyst, time of day, recent tracked performance of the setup); A grades receive maximum planned risk, lower grades reduced or zero size. Grades are audited in daily review against outcomes per grade.
failure_modes: Grade inflation under overconfidence or FOMO turns marginal trades into 'A-trades'; without per-grade outcome tracking the label is decoration. Even genuine A-setups lose often - the grade governs size, not the result.
misconceptions: An A-trade is not a guaranteed winner; it is a bet-sizing category grounded in historical expectancy of the pattern class. Confidence felt in the moment is not a grading criterion.
example: Earnings-gap momentum continuation with triple relative volume in a trending tape grades A and takes the full 1R risk; the same pattern pre-market in thin volume does not.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: B-trade
definition: In the A/B/C setup-grading taxonomy used in proprietary trading, a valid playbook setup taken under only partially favorable conditions - worth trading but at reduced size relative to an A-trade. It is the middle tier of the setup-quality hierarchy that links conviction to position size.
intuition: The pattern is right but the context is average - you can play it, just not with A-trade money.
mechanics: A setup meeting playbook definitions but missing some confluence (weaker trend alignment, mediocre volume, suboptimal time of day) is graded B and traded at a fraction of full risk, preserving capital for A opportunities. Per-grade outcome tracking in review keeps the grade boundaries honest.
failure_modes: Under emotional pressure, B-trades get relabeled as A-trades for size, or skipped entirely after losses; both corrupt the sizing logic the taxonomy exists to enforce. B-trades also have thinner expectancy, so execution slippage hurts them proportionally more.
misconceptions: A B-trade is not a bad trade - it is a smaller bet on a positive but lower-expectancy instance. Trading B-setups at full size, not trading them at all, is the common mistake.
example: A clean pullback pattern in a directionless midday tape grades B: tradable at half size because the pattern is right but the context is average.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: C-trade
definition: The lowest grade in the A/B/C setup taxonomy used in proprietary trading: a marginal or borderline opportunity that technically resembles a playbook setup but lacks confluence, so its historical expectancy does not cover costs. Standard practice is to skip C-trades or trade them only at minimal, exploratory size.
intuition: A C-trade is a trade you take because you are bored or afraid of missing out - the grade exists so you recognize it and pass.
mechanics: Borderline instances of playbook patterns - weak volume, wrong time of day, choppy context - are graded C, which in a disciplined framework means no trade or minimal size. Tracking C-grade outcomes in review typically confirms that skipping them adds to net expectancy by cutting cost bleed.
failure_modes: C-trades are where overtrading and FOMO actually enter the account: each is individually small, but their aggregate cost and negative expectancy erode the edge earned on A and B setups. Grading discipline collapses first on quiet days, when C-setups are most tempting.
misconceptions: Skipping C-trades is not excessive caution - when a pattern's tracked expectancy is below costs, not trading is the profitable decision. A C-grade that wins is still a C-grade.
example: A breakout with no volume confirmation late on a quiet Friday grades C and is passed; its tracked expectancy over similar past instances was negative after costs.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: Daily review
definition: An end-of-day routine in which the day's trades are logged, graded against plan rules, and analyzed for errors and lessons before the next session. It is the shortest feedback loop in the trading process and the primary driver of incremental improvement.
intuition: Ten honest minutes with the day's trades each evening is worth more than ten hours of new course material.
mechanics: Typical steps: reconcile fills, tag each trade by setup, score rule adherence, classify errors (analysis, execution, risk), note emotional state, and write one or two actionable lessons; results feed the weekly review. Professional prop desks institutionalize recorded daily trade review.
failure_modes: It is skipped on losing days - when it matters most - or degrades into P&L checking, losing its function. The opposite failure is overreacting to a single day's noise by rewriting rules nightly.
misconceptions: Daily review is not about judging the day's profit; one day is almost pure variance. It is also not optional maintenance - it is where plan, journal, and psychology connect.
example: After the close a trader replays his three trades, tags one as a C-setup he should not have taken, notes he hesitated on a valid entry, and writes both into tomorrow's pre-market notes.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents (trader education and review practices)

name: Weekly review
definition: A weekly aggregation and analysis of the trading journal - process metrics, outcome statistics by setup, recurring errors, and psychological patterns - used to adjust the playbook and plan on a sample less noisy than daily results. It produces a small number of concrete, testable adjustments rather than wholesale rewrites.
intuition: Days are noise; the week is the first window where your actual habits become visible as data.
mechanics: Compiles the week's trades: adherence rate, expectancy and R-distribution per setup, error counts by type, best and worst conditions; conclusions become at most a few documented changes (drop a setup, cap a time window, adjust a review step), which are then tracked for effect in subsequent weeks.
failure_modes: A week is still a small sample - structural strategy changes on five days of data are overfitting to noise. Reviews without structured journal data become mood summaries rather than analysis.
misconceptions: Weekly review is not a performance verdict; it is hypothesis generation for the plan. Nor is more analysis always better - the output should be a short list of testable adjustments.
example: Friday's review shows all of the week's losses came from opening-range trades taken before 9:45; the plan is amended to exclude that window and the change is re-evaluated the following week.

citations.source: Brett N. Steenbarger, The Psychology of Trading: Tools and Techniques for Minding the Markets (Wiley, 2003) - publisher page

name: Playbook
definition: A trader's curated, documented collection of proven setups - each with context conditions, entry, exit, sizing, and a worked example - built from personal trading results and reviewed regularly. Popularized by Mike Bellafiore (One Good Trade; The PlayBook), it turns scattered experience into an explicit library of tradable patterns.
intuition: Instead of trading everything the market shows you, you trade only the handful of patterns you have written down, tested, and own.
mechanics: Each playbook entry documents one setup: market context, trigger, invalidation, targets, sizing rule, and annotated screenshots from real trades; entries are added from review of one's own best trades and retired when tracked expectancy decays. Setup-quality grading (A/B/C) is applied against playbook definitions.
failure_modes: Playbooks ossify: setups fitted to one market regime keep being traded after the regime ends, so each entry needs ongoing expectancy tracking. Copying another trader's playbook without one's own screen time and data usually fails.
misconceptions: A playbook is not a list of chart patterns from a book; it is a personal, evidence-backed subset of what that trader executes best. More setups is not better - depth in a few beats breadth.
example: A trader's playbook holds four setups; when his quarterly review shows one has been negative for 60 trades, it is retired and replaced by a pattern his journal shows emerging.

citations.source: Mike Bellafiore, One Good Trade: Inside the Highly Competitive World of Proprietary Trading (Wiley, 2010) - publisher page
citations.section: Book description and table of contents

name: Trading routine
definition: The fixed daily and weekly structure around trading - pre-market preparation, defined session behaviors, post-market review - that standardizes decision quality and conserves willpower. Routines externalize discipline into schedule and environment instead of relying on in-the-moment self-control.
intuition: You cannot will yourself into consistency every day; you build a routine so the consistent behavior happens by default.
mechanics: Typical elements: pre-market plan (levels, catalysts, scenarios), warm-up and state check, session rules (trading windows, breaks, loss limits), a shutdown ritual, daily review, and sleep and exercise management. Trading-psychology work such as Steenbarger's emphasizes structured practice and self-coaching routines as the mechanism of trader development.
failure_modes: Routines decay under travel, stress, or overconfidence after good stretches, usually starting with skipped preparation. An overly rigid routine also breaks when market conditions shift the session structure, as on event days.
misconceptions: A routine is not superstition or comfort ritual; its components exist to control preparation quality, arousal, and exposure. Watching screens longer is not a routine - it is often the absence of one.
example: A trader's day: 7:00 review of overnight markets and scenarios, 9:20 checklist and state check, trade only 9:30-11:00, hard daily stop at -2R, journal and review by 16:30 - the same sequence every session.

citations.source: Brett N. Steenbarger, The Psychology of Trading: Tools and Techniques for Minding the Markets (Wiley, 2003) - publisher page

name: Mental stop
definition: A stop-loss level held in the trader's mind rather than placed as an order with the broker: the trader commits to exit manually if price reaches the level. It preserves flexibility and avoids order visibility but depends entirely on real-time discipline under stress.
intuition: A mental stop is a promise to yourself; the market will test exactly your willingness to keep it.
mechanics: The invalidation level is defined at entry but no resting order is working; when price trades there, the trader must execute the exit manually, which introduces hesitation risk, delay slippage, and the temptation to renegotiate. It is the discretionary counterpart of the hard stop, which is an actual stop or stop-limit order resting at the venue.
failure_modes: It fails precisely when needed most: fast markets, news spikes, and tilt states, where the trader freezes, moves the level, or averages down instead. Without a working order, gaps and connectivity failures leave the position unprotected.
misconceptions: Mental stops are not 'more professional'; they are appropriate mainly for experienced traders in liquid markets who watch the position continuously. Honoring a mental stop nine times out of ten still leaves the tenth - often the catastrophic one.
example: Long from 50 with a mental stop at 48.50; a surprise headline dumps the stock through the level in seconds and the trader, hesitating, exits at 47.90 - triple the planned slippage.

citations.source: Wikipedia: Order (exchange)
citations.section: Stop order / stop-loss order mechanics (the exchange-level mechanism a mental stop forgoes)

name: Hard stop
definition: A stop-loss instruction resting with the broker or exchange as an actual order (stop or stop-limit), which triggers automatically when price reaches the stop level. It enforces the invalidation point mechanically, removing real-time discretion - at the cost of possible slippage or non-fill in fast markets.
intuition: A hard stop is the exit decision executed by the machine, so the future, emotional version of you does not get a vote.
mechanics: A sell-stop sits below the market (a buy-stop above it, for shorts); when the stop price trades, a stop order becomes a market order - execution guaranteed, price not - while a stop-limit becomes a limit order - price capped, execution not. Trailing-stop variants ratchet the stop with favorable price movement.
failure_modes: In gaps and fast markets a stop-market fills far through the stop price, and a stop-limit may not fill at all; obvious stop levels can be run by short-term liquidity hunts before the move resumes. A hard stop does not cap gap risk.
misconceptions: A stop-loss does not guarantee the exit price - 'stop' is a trigger, not a fill price. Nor are hard stops only for the undisciplined; they are structural risk control that survives distraction, outages, and emotional episodes.
example: Long 250 shares at 50 with a sell-stop at 48 (planned -$500 risk); an overnight gap opens at 47.20 and the stop market-fills at 47.25 - more than planned, but bounded and automatic.

citations.source: Wikipedia: Order (exchange)
citations.section: Stop order; stop-limit order; trailing stop order

name: Trading hypothesis
definition: A falsifiable statement that specified market information and trading rules are associated with a measurable outcome under stated timing, cost, and risk assumptions.
intuition: It turns an informal trading idea into a claim or design choice that can be evaluated against dated evidence.
mechanics: State the information set, decision rule, forecast horizon, instruments, benchmark, costs, and rejection criterion before evaluating dated data.
failure_modes: Results can mislead when hindsight, multiple testing, nonstationarity, costs, or unavailable historical information are ignored.
misconceptions: A favorable historical result is evidence about the tested sample and assumptions, not proof of a durable profitable edge.
example: Hypothesis: stocks with positive 12-month momentum outperform the equal-weight universe over the next month after 20 basis points of round-trip costs.

citations.source: CFA Institute, Backtesting & Simulation
citations.section: Summary: rolling-window backtesting, bias, simulation, and sensitivity analysis

name: Signal
definition: A dated numeric or categorical output that a trading process uses to express expected return, risk, or an intended action.
intuition: It turns an informal trading idea into a claim or design choice that can be evaluated against dated evidence.
mechanics: Compute it only from information available at the decision timestamp, then map its value to a forecast, rank, or order rule.
failure_modes: Results can mislead when hindsight, multiple testing, nonstationarity, costs, or unavailable historical information are ignored.
misconceptions: A favorable historical result is evidence about the tested sample and assumptions, not proof of a durable profitable edge.
example: A five-day return of +4% produces a +1 momentum signal and a target long position at the next tradable price.

citations.source: CFA Institute, Backtesting & Simulation
citations.section: Summary: rolling-window backtesting, bias, simulation, and sensitivity analysis

name: Feature
definition: An input variable supplied to a statistical or machine-learning model, derived from raw observations without using future information.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Define its timestamp and lookback, fit any transformation on training data, and construct the same value identically in validation and live use.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: At each close, 20-day realized volatility computed through that close is a feature for predicting next-day range.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Dataset transformations

name: Label
definition: The observed class or value assigned to an example as the outcome a supervised model is trained to predict.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Define the event window and labeling rule, align it after the feature timestamp, and prevent overlapping outcomes from leaking across splits.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: A row dated Monday receives label 1 if Tuesday's close-to-close return is positive and 0 otherwise.

name: Target variable
definition: The response variable whose conditional value, probability, or class a supervised model is fitted to estimate.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Choose an economically meaningful horizon, construct it from future outcomes relative to each feature row, and exclude it from the input columns.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: For a regression model, the target is the next five-day excess return in decimal form.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation

name: Training set
definition: The observations used to estimate model parameters and fit data-dependent transformations.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Restrict fitting, feature selection, scaling, and imputation to these rows before applying the learned operations elsewhere.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: A 2015-2021 sample fits a scaler and classifier; no 2022 values enter either fit.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation

name: Validation set
definition: Held-out observations used during development to compare models, tune hyperparameters, or choose stopping points.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Evaluate candidate choices on this set while keeping the final test set untouched until the design is frozen.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Models with depths 2, 4, and 8 are trained on 2015-2020 and compared on 2021 validation data.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation
citations.section: Training, validation, test sets and cross-validation

name: Test set
definition: A final held-out sample used once to estimate performance after model and hyperparameter choices are fixed.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Lock the pipeline first, apply it without refitting to the test observations, and report all prespecified metrics and costs.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: After choosing depth on 2021 validation data, the frozen model is evaluated once on 2022-2023 test data.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation
citations.section: Training, validation, test sets and cross-validation

name: In-sample period
definition: The historical interval used directly to design, fit, select, or calibrate a strategy or model.
intuition: It turns an informal trading idea into a claim or design choice that can be evaluated against dated evidence.
mechanics: Record the interval and every decision influenced by it; treat performance from it as development evidence rather than an independent test.
failure_modes: Results can mislead when hindsight, multiple testing, nonstationarity, costs, or unavailable historical information are ignored.
misconceptions: A favorable historical result is evidence about the tested sample and assumptions, not proof of a durable profitable edge.
example: Parameters chosen using 2015-2020 make that entire interval in-sample even if only part was used for fitting.

citations.source: SEC, Investment Adviser Advertisements; Compensation for Solicitations

name: Out-of-sample period
definition: A later or otherwise untouched interval not used to formulate, fit, or select the evaluated strategy.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Freeze the design before revealing results, simulate decisions using only contemporaneously available data, and disclose any later reuse for tuning.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: A strategy finalized with data through 2021 is first evaluated on 2022-2023, making those years out-of-sample for that test.

citations.source: SEC, Investment Adviser Advertisements; Compensation for Solicitations

name: Backtest
definition: A historical simulation that applies explicit strategy rules to past data to estimate how the strategy would have behaved under stated assumptions.
intuition: It turns an informal trading idea into a claim or design choice that can be evaluated against dated evidence.
mechanics: Advance through dated observations, form decisions from the contemporaneous information set, simulate orders and costs, and update cash and positions.
failure_modes: Results can mislead when hindsight, multiple testing, nonstationarity, costs, or unavailable historical information are ignored.
misconceptions: A favorable historical result is evidence about the tested sample and assumptions, not proof of a durable profitable edge.
example: A monthly momentum rule is replayed from 2010 through 2020 with delisted stocks, next-open fills, fees, and slippage.

name: Event-driven backtest
definition: A backtest in which a clock processes market, signal, order, fill, and portfolio events in timestamp order.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Each event updates state and may enqueue later events, preventing strategy logic from reading beyond the current time frontier.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A 09:30 quote triggers an order event; a later trade event partially fills it and then updates cash.

name: Vectorized backtest
definition: A backtest that computes signals, positions, and returns primarily as aligned array operations rather than replaying individual events.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Construct lagged positions and return series, align them explicitly, and apply turnover and cost adjustments across the arrays.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: Daily signal s at row t is shifted one row before multiplying return r at t, preventing same-close look-ahead.

name: Walk-forward analysis
definition: Sequential evaluation that repeatedly fits or selects a model on past data and tests the frozen result on the next unseen time block.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Move the training and test boundaries forward, refit only on data preceding each test block, and concatenate the non-overlapping test results.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Fit on 2018-2020 and test 2021, then fit on 2019-2021 and test 2022.

name: Rolling-window analysis
definition: Walk-forward analysis whose training window has fixed length and drops the oldest observations as it advances.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Choose train and test lengths, fit on each trailing window, and evaluate on the immediately following block.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Use the prior 36 months to fit each model and predict the next month, then roll both boundaries forward one month.

name: Expanding-window analysis
definition: Walk-forward analysis whose training set begins at a fixed origin and grows as each new block becomes available.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Fit on all observations up to a cutoff, test on the next block, add that block to training, and repeat.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Fit through 2020 and test 2021; then fit through 2021 and test 2022.

name: Forward test
definition: Prospective evaluation of a frozen strategy on market data that arrives after development, without risking capital necessarily.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Version the rules, parameters, and code; record signals and simulated fills as new data arrive; compare results with prespecified expectations.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: A strategy frozen on June 30 produces timestamped shadow orders from July through December before any launch decision.

name: Paper trading
definition: Running a strategy against live or delayed market data with simulated orders and account balances instead of real executions and capital.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Submit orders to a simulated brokerage model, record assumed fills, fees, and buying power, and reconcile those assumptions with observable markets.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A paper account buys 100 shares, but its immediate full fill is flagged as optimistic because only 20 shares were displayed.

name: Shadow trading
definition: A prospective test that generates and records production-intended orders alongside a live process but does not route those orders for execution.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Feed the production data stream through frozen logic, retain intended order timestamps and quantities, and compare them with executable quotes and actual system latency.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A shadow strategy logs a 10:00:00 buy and later measures the ask available when the order would have reached the venue.

name: Live trading
definition: Execution of a strategy using current market data and real orders, capital, fills, fees, and operational constraints.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Receive streaming data, create and route orders, handle asynchronous fills and failures, update portfolio state, and monitor risk controls.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A live limit order receives two partial fills and the strategy updates its remaining quantity after each broker event.

name: Backtest engine
definition: Software that coordinates historical data, the simulation clock, strategy callbacks, order state, portfolio accounting, and performance output.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Load dated data, enforce a time frontier, dispatch events or bars, call strategy logic, pass orders to reality models, and persist results.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: The engine advances to 10:01, invokes the algorithm, sends its order to a fill model, and books the returned execution.

name: Execution simulator
definition: The backtest component that converts hypothetical orders into timestamped fills or rejections under explicit market and brokerage assumptions.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Apply venue hours, order-type rules, latency, available price and volume, partial-fill logic, costs, and market impact before returning execution events.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A 5,000-share market order is capped at 10% of bar volume and fills over several bars with impact.

name: Fill model
definition: A rule set that determines whether, when, at what price, and in what quantity a simulated order executes.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Evaluate the order type against eligible post-order market data, enforce price conditions, and emit full, partial, or no fill with a timestamp.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.

name: Commission model
definition: A model that deducts broker, exchange, clearing, and regulatory charges from simulated trading results.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Map each fill's venue, instrument, quantity, price, side, and account tier to a fee, then debit it when the fill is booked.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.

name: Slippage model
definition: A model of the difference between a decision or reference price and the simulated execution price attributable to spread, delay, liquidity, and impact.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Estimate an adverse price adjustment from order size, volume, volatility, latency, or a calibrated constant and apply it to the fill price.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A buy order with 8 basis points of modeled slippage fills at 100.08 when the reference price is 100.

name: Market-impact model
definition: A model of price movement caused by the strategy's own trading, often separated into temporary and persistent components.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Estimate impact from participation, order size, volatility, liquidity, execution time, and calibrated coefficients; feed it into simulated fills and later prices if modeled.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A 10% participation order receives more impact than a 1% participation order in the same stock and volatility regime.

name: Borrow-cost model
definition: A model of fees and constraints incurred when maintaining short positions in borrowed securities.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: For each short position, apply the dated borrow rate and availability to market value over elapsed time, accrue the charge, and reject or recall unavailable borrow when modeled.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: Borrowing $100,000 of stock for 30 days at 6% annualized accrues about $493 on an actual/365 basis.

name: Funding-cost model
definition: A model of interest paid or received on financed cash balances, margin, or derivative funding exposures.
intuition: It is part of the machinery that converts strategy instructions into simulated positions, cash flows, and performance.
mechanics: Apply the relevant dated rate, spread, balance, and day-count convention over each accrual interval and post the cash flow.
failure_modes: Simplified timing, liquidity, fee, borrow, funding, or corporate-action assumptions can make simulated results unattainable live.
misconceptions: A detailed simulator reduces modeling error but cannot reproduce every queue event or future market condition.
example: A $200,000 debit balance funded for 10 days at 7% annualized costs about $384 on an actual/365 basis.

name: Corporate-action adjustment
definition: The point-in-time treatment of splits, dividends, mergers, spinoffs, and other issuer events in prices, positions, orders, and cash flows.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: On the event's effective timestamp, adjust quantities and reference prices or book the economic distribution without using later-known terms early.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: A 2-for-1 split changes 100 shares at a $60 basis into 200 shares at a $30 per-share basis without creating profit.

name: Point-in-time data
definition: Historical data stored as it was known or effective at each past decision time, including vintage dates and later revisions.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: For every value and universe membership, select the version whose release timestamp was no later than the simulated decision timestamp.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: A March backtest uses the GDP estimate released in February, not the revised value published in June.

name: Data revision
definition: A later correction, restatement, benchmark update, or methodological change to a previously released observation.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Store vintages and release times, use the then-available version in simulation, and separately test sensitivity to revised history.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: An earnings value reported as $1.00 in April and restated to $0.80 in August remains $1.00 for a May decision simulation.

citations.source: CFA Institute Research Foundation, Investment Model Validation

name: Data cleaning
definition: The documented process of detecting and handling invalid, inconsistent, duplicate, missing, or mistimed observations before analysis.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Define rules from domain knowledge, preserve raw data and audit flags, fit statistical thresholds on training data, and test the effect of each correction.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: A negative share volume is flagged invalid and set missing rather than silently converted to a positive number.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Dataset transformations

name: Data normalization
definition: A broad transformation that puts observations into a chosen scale or norm so features can be compared or consumed reliably by a model.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Fit transformation parameters on training observations and apply the stored mapping unchanged to validation, test, and live rows.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: Each return vector is divided by its L2 norm before a similarity model, while the fitted pipeline is reused out of sample.

name: Standardization
definition: Feature-wise centering and scaling, conventionally subtracting the training mean and dividing by the training standard deviation.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Estimate mean and scale on training rows, store them, and transform every later row with those same values.
formula: z = (x - training mean) / training standard deviation
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: Training values 8, 10, and 12 have mean 10 and standard deviation about 1.63, so 12 maps to about 1.22.

name: Min-max scaling
definition: A linear transformation mapping the training minimum and maximum of a feature to a specified range, commonly zero to one.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Estimate the extrema on training data and apply the same affine transform out of sample, allowing later values to fall outside the range unless clipped.
formula: x_scaled = (x - min_train) / (max_train - min_train)
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: With training minimum 10 and maximum 30, value 20 maps to 0.5 and later value 40 maps to 1.5.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Preprocessing data

name: Winsorization
definition: Capping observations below and above chosen quantiles or limits at those boundary values rather than deleting them.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Choose limits from training data, replace lower and upper tail values with the respective caps, and reuse the caps on later data.
formula: x_w = min(max(x, lower_cap), upper_cap)
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: With caps at -5 and 5, observations -9, 2, and 8 become -5, 2, and 5.

name: Feature engineering
definition: Creating model inputs from raw data through domain-informed transformations, aggregations, interactions, lags, or encodings.
intuition: It controls what information the model receives and in what numerical representation.
mechanics: Specify each feature's information timestamp and window, implement it in a train/live-consistent pipeline, and test it without fitting on future rows.
failure_modes: Fitting the operation on the full dataset leaks future information; revisions, outliers, and missing values can also distort results.
misconceptions: A cleaner or rescaled dataset is not automatically more truthful; transformations must preserve timing and economic meaning.
example: Daily closes are converted into lagged 5-day return, 20-day volatility, and price-to-moving-average features.

name: Feature selection
definition: Choosing a subset of candidate inputs using prespecified statistical, model-based, or domain criteria.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Fit the selector inside each training fold, apply it to that fold's validation data, and repeat selection when the training window changes.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Within each fold, the 10 highest training-set mutual-information features are selected from 200 candidates.

name: Cross-validation
definition: A resampling procedure that repeatedly fits a model on one subset and evaluates it on held-out observations to estimate generalization and compare choices.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Choose a splitter consistent with the data-generating process, fit the entire pipeline inside each training fold, score each held-out fold, and aggregate the scores.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Five-fold cross-validation trains on four folds and scores the fifth five times, so every row is evaluated out of fold once.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide, Cross-validation

name: Time-series cross-validation
definition: Cross-validation whose splits preserve chronology so training observations precede the observations used for evaluation.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Create sequential train/test index pairs, optionally cap the training window and insert a gap, fit on past rows, and score the next block.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Train on months 1-24 and test 25-30, then train on 1-30 and test 31-36.

name: Purged cross-validation
definition: A time-series cross-validation design that removes training observations whose label-information intervals overlap a test fold.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Represent each sample by its information start and label end, create a test fold, then purge any training interval that intersects the test intervals.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: If a Friday label uses returns through Wednesday, training rows whose labels also use that Monday-Wednesday interval are removed when Friday is tested.

name: Embargo period
definition: A buffer excluded from training around or after a test interval to reduce leakage from serial dependence or overlapping information sets.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: After assigning the test interval, exclude the prescribed number or percentage of adjacent observations from the eligible training indices.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: A five-day embargo after a March test fold prevents early-April rows from entering that fold's training set.

citations.source: A Bayesian-based classification framework for financial time series trend prediction

name: Hyperparameter
definition: A model or training setting chosen outside the parameter-fitting procedure, such as tree depth, regularization strength, or learning rate.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Define a search space, estimate each candidate with training-fold validation, select under a stated objective, and preserve a final untouched test.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: Tree depths 2, 4, and 6 are hyperparameter candidates; depth 4 is selected by mean validation log loss.

name: Grid search
definition: Hyperparameter search that evaluates every point in a finite Cartesian product of candidate values.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Enumerate all combinations, evaluate each through the same cross-validation pipeline and metric, then refit the selected combination on the development data.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Three learning rates times four tree depths produce 12 configurations, each evaluated on the same time folds.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide
citations.section: Supervised learning, unsupervised learning, model selection, and inspection

name: Random search
definition: Hyperparameter search that samples a fixed number of configurations from specified distributions rather than exhaustively enumerating a grid.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Specify distributions and a random seed, draw the budgeted configurations, evaluate each consistently, and select by the prespecified score.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Twenty pairs of log-uniform learning rate and integer tree depth are drawn from a space containing thousands of possibilities.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide
citations.section: Supervised learning, unsupervised learning, model selection, and inspection

name: Bayesian optimization
definition: Sequential hyperparameter optimization that uses a probabilistic surrogate of prior evaluations to choose promising next configurations.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: Fit a surrogate to evaluated configurations and scores, maximize an acquisition function, run the proposed trial, and update the surrogate until the budget ends.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: After eight initial trials, expected improvement proposes a lower learning rate near the best observed region for trial nine.

citations.source: scikit-learn User Guide
citations.section: Supervised learning, unsupervised learning, model selection, and inspection

name: Objective function
definition: A scalar criterion that fitting or optimization seeks to minimize or maximize, optionally combining data loss and penalties.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Compute the criterion from predictions, targets, parameters, and constraints; use its gradient or search comparisons to update the candidate solution.
formula: Objective = data loss + regularization penalty
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A model minimizes validation log loss plus 0.01 times the sum of squared weights.

name: Constraint
definition: A condition that restricts the feasible parameters, predictions, portfolio weights, or decisions available to an optimization.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Express the restriction as bounds, equalities, inequalities, or admissible sets and search only solutions that satisfy them.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.

name: Regularization
definition: A fitting technique that discourages model complexity through penalties, shrinkage, structural restrictions, or noise to improve generalization.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Add a complexity penalty or constraint to the training objective, tune its strength on validation data, and refit without using test results.
formula: Regularized objective = empirical loss + lambda times penalty
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: Increasing an L2 penalty from 0 to 0.1 shrinks a fitted coefficient from 2.4 to 1.7.

name: Early stopping
definition: Terminating iterative training when a monitored held-out metric stops improving, thereby limiting effective model complexity.
intuition: It estimates how a fitted choice behaves on observations that were not used to fit that choice.
mechanics: After each iteration, evaluate a validation metric, retain the best checkpoint, and stop after a preset patience without sufficient improvement.
failure_modes: Random splitting, overlapping labels, repeated tuning, or an unprotected final test set can produce optimistic estimates.
misconceptions: Validation measures conditional generalization under a split design; it does not guarantee future market performance.
example: Validation loss bottoms at epoch 42 and fails to improve for 10 epochs, so training stops at 52 and restores epoch 42.

name: Ensemble model
definition: A predictor that combines outputs from multiple component models to improve stability, accuracy, or coverage of different patterns.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Train diverse base estimators and aggregate their predictions by averaging, voting, weighted blending, or a learned meta-model.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.

name: Bagging
definition: An ensemble method that fits base estimators independently on resampled observations or features and averages or votes their predictions.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Draw bootstrap samples, train one base model per sample, obtain predictions from all models, and aggregate them.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.

name: Boosting
definition: An additive ensemble method that trains weak learners sequentially so later learners emphasize errors or negative gradients left by the current ensemble.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Initialize a prediction, fit a learner to weighted errors or loss gradients, scale its contribution, and add it to the ensemble repeatedly.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A second stump focuses on observations misclassified by the first and its weighted vote is added to the score.

citations.source: scikit-learn API, ensemble methods

name: Random forest
definition: A bagged ensemble of decision trees that also randomizes the candidate features considered at splits, reducing correlation among trees.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Bootstrap rows for each tree, choose splits from random feature subsets, grow many trees, then average regression values or vote on classes.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: Five hundred trees each consider sqrt(p) features per split; 310 vote for an up day, producing class 1.

citations.source: scikit-learn API, ensemble methods

name: Gradient boosting
definition: Boosting that adds weak learners fitted to the negative gradient of a differentiable loss with respect to current predictions.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Compute current predictions and loss gradients, fit a small tree to those gradients, scale it by a learning rate, and add it to the model.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A regression tree fitted to residual-like gradients is multiplied by 0.05 and added as iteration 20.

citations.source: scikit-learn API, ensemble methods

name: XGBoost
definition: A scalable gradient-tree-boosting system using a regularized objective, second-order loss approximation, sparsity-aware split handling, and optimized tree construction.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: At each boosting round, use gradients and Hessians to choose tree splits and leaf weights, add the regularized tree, and update predictions.
formula: Prediction = sum of tree leaf scores; objective = loss + sum of tree penalties
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A binary classifier adds 200 shallow trees at learning rate 0.05 and converts the summed margin through a logistic link.

name: Neural network
definition: A parameterized composition of affine transformations and nonlinear activations trained to approximate a mapping from inputs to outputs.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Run inputs forward through layers, compute a loss, propagate gradients backward, and update weights with an optimizer over repeated batches.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A network maps 20 features through 32 ReLU units to one sigmoid probability and updates weights using minibatch gradients.

name: Recurrent neural network
definition: A neural network for sequences that updates a hidden state from the current input and previous state, sharing parameters across time steps.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Process observations in order using h_t = activation(W_x x_t + W_h h_previous + b), then map states to outputs and train through time.
formula: h_t = f(W_x x_t + W_h h_(t-1) + b)
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A 30-day return sequence updates one hidden state per day and the final state predicts day 31 direction.

citations.source: Keras API, Recurrent layers

name: Long short-term memory network
definition: A gated recurrent neural network whose cell state and input, forget, and output gates regulate information retention across long sequences.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: At each time step compute gate values, update the cell state from retained and candidate information, then expose a gated hidden state.
formula: c_t = f_t c_(t-1) + i_t g_t; h_t = o_t tanh(c_t)
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: An LSTM reads 60 daily feature vectors and uses its final hidden state to forecast the next five-day return.

citations.source: Keras API, Recurrent layers

name: Transformer model
definition: A sequence model built from attention and position-wise transformations rather than recurrent state updates.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Embed inputs with position information, apply multi-head self-attention and feed-forward blocks with residual connections and normalization, then map outputs to the task.
formula: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A Transformer attends across 128 return observations in parallel and pools the encoded sequence for classification.

name: Attention mechanism
definition: A differentiable operation that forms each output as a weighted combination of value vectors, with weights derived from compatibility between queries and keys.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Compute query-key scores, scale and normalize them with softmax, then multiply the resulting weights by values; multiple heads learn different projections.
formula: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
example: A query for the current day assigns 60% of its weight to a recent volatility shock and smaller weights to other days.

name: Classification
definition: A supervised-learning task that maps inputs to one of a finite set of labels or estimates probabilities over those labels.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Fit a decision function or class-probability model on labeled training examples, choose any operating threshold on validation data, and evaluate held out outcomes.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.

name: Regression task
definition: A supervised-learning task that estimates a continuous numeric target from input features.
intuition: It is a learnable mapping or representation used to turn features into predictions or groups.
mechanics: Fit a function by minimizing a regression loss on training data and evaluate numeric prediction errors on temporally held-out observations.
failure_modes: Flexible models can fit noise, shift under new regimes, and conceal instability when tuning is repeated on the same validation data.
misconceptions: Greater model complexity or in-sample accuracy does not by itself imply better out-of-sample trading results.
